# **Engineering Monograph: 2D to 3D Spatial Audio Conversion and Binaural Rendering Architecture**

## **PART I: Terminology and Fundamentals**

The transition from conventional audio representations to immersive spatial audio requires a rigorous understanding of channel-based, object-based, and scene-based paradigms.  
Mono audio consists of a single channel, carrying no spatial information other than what might be inferred from intrinsic reverberation and spectral roll-off. Stereo audio utilizes two discrete channels (left and right), relying on amplitude panning to create a one-dimensional phantom image between two loudspeakers. Multichannel audio expands this horizontally; the 5.1 format adds a center channel and two surround channels alongside a low-frequency effects (LFE) channel, while 7.1 adds rear surrounds. Immersive multichannel formats introduce elevation: 7.1.4 adds four overhead speakers, and 9.1.6 adds additional front-wide and overhead speakers for greater hemispherical resolution1.  
Channel-based audio is strictly tied to a specific loudspeaker layout. In contrast, object-based audio abstracts the audio signal from the reproduction layout. An audio object comprises the raw pulse-code modulation (PCM) signal and dynamic metadata representing its Cartesian coordinates, spatial spread, and volume2. The object renderer calculates the necessary panning coefficients for the user's specific loudspeaker or headphone setup at playback, ensuring layout-agnostic reproduction.  
Scene-based audio, primarily Ambisonics, represents the acoustic soundfield as a set of spherical harmonics3. First-order Ambisonics (FOA) uses four channels to represent the omnidirectional pressure and the three directional velocity components. Higher Order Ambisonics (HOA) increases the spatial resolution by adding higher-degree spherical harmonic components, effectively reducing the spatial aliasing frequency5.  
Binaural audio specifically targets headphone reproduction, utilizing Head-Related Transfer Functions (HRTFs) to simulate the acoustic filtering of the human head, torso, and pinnae. Headphone virtualization algorithms synthesize virtual loudspeakers around the listener by processing standard channel-based signals (like 7.1) through HRTF convolution. Conversely, Wave Field Synthesis (WFS) relies on the Huygens-Fresnel principle, utilizing massive loudspeaker arrays to physically synthesize acoustic wave-fronts, creating a true physical soundfield rather than a psychoacoustic illusion. Acoustic scene analysis refers to the computational extraction of spatial and semantic properties from these audio formats, forming the foundation for automated spatialization.

## **PART II: Human Spatial Hearing**

Human auditory localization relies on a combination of time, intensity, and spectral cues, processed synergistically by the auditory cortex.  
The Interaural Time Difference (ITD) is the primary cue for localizing low-frequency sounds (below approximately 1.5 kHz) in the horizontal plane (azimuth). The ITD arises from the path length difference between the two ears. A classical approximation is the Woodworth model, which assumes a rigid spherical head. For a sound source at azimuth ![][image1], the ITD is defined mathematically by the extra distance the sound must travel around the sphere to reach the contralateral ear.  
The Interaural Level Difference (ILD) dominates at higher frequencies (above 1.5 kHz). The physical head acts as an acoustic baffle, creating a head shadow that attenuates high frequencies arriving at the contralateral ear. ILD is highly frequency-dependent and non-linear. Together, ITD and ILD define a "cone of confusion"—a locus of spatial coordinates yielding identical interaural differences.  
Spectral cues are strictly required to resolve this cone of confusion, enabling front/back disambiguation and elevation perception. The physical geometry of the pinna introduces highly directional comb-filtering effects. Specifically, pinna notches (spectral dips between 5 kHz and 12 kHz) shift in frequency depending on the source elevation7. Torso reflections further provide low-frequency comb-filtering cues for elevation.  
Distance perception relies on multiple interacting physical phenomena. The inverse-square law dictates that acoustic intensity drops by 6 dB per doubling of distance in a free field. Frequency-dependent air absorption acts as a low-pass filter over vast distances. Crucially, the direct-to-reverberant ratio (DRR) serves as a primary absolute distance cue; as a source recedes, direct energy falls while reverberant energy remains statistically constant. In the extreme near-field (under 1 meter), the proximity effect generates exaggerated ILDs, particularly at low frequencies, which the brain interprets as extreme closeness.  
The precedence effect (or Haas effect) describes the auditory system's tendency to localize a sound source based solely on the first arriving wavefront, suppressing the directional information of subsequent reflections arriving within 1 to 40 milliseconds. This evolutionary mechanism prevents confusing echoes in reverberant environments from destroying localization accuracy.  
The Binaural Masking Level Difference (BMLD) demonstrates the auditory system's ability to unmask a signal from noise using interaural phase differences (IPD). If a signal and noise are diotic (identical at both ears, denoted ![][image2]), detectability is poor. Inverting the phase of the signal at one ear (![][image3]) can improve the detection threshold by up to 15 dB8. High-quality spatial DSP must preserve accurate phase relationships to maintain this spatial unmasking capability, which directly affects speech intelligibility in complex scenes.  
Without these synthesized cues, headphone listening results in in-head localization, where the audio is perceived inside the listener's skull. Externalization requires the precise combination of ITD, ILD, pinna cues, and room reflections.

## **PART III: HRTF — Extremely Detailed**

The Head-Related Transfer Function, ![][image4], mathematically encapsulates the ITD, ILD, and spectral cues for a given azimuth, elevation, and distance. It is the frequency-domain representation of the Head-Related Impulse Response (HRIR), ![][image5].  
HRIRs are obtained via empirical measurements in anechoic chambers using a dummy head (such as KEMAR) or human subjects equipped with miniature in-ear microphones4. A loudspeaker mounted on a robotic hoop generates a logarithmic sine sweep, which is recorded by the microphones and deconvolved to extract the impulse response of the acoustic path.  
Because raw HRIRs contain the measurement equipment's coloration (loudspeaker and microphone responses), they must be equalized. Furthermore, direct interpolation between adjacent raw HRIRs in the time domain causes destructive phase cancellation (comb filtering) due to the varying arrival times (ITDs). To solve this, modern DSP pipelines decompose the HRIR into a minimum-phase component and a pure delay component11.  
A minimum-phase filter contains all the spectral magnitude information (and thus the ILD and pinna cues) but removes the ITD, concentrating the energy at the beginning of the impulse response. The ITD is extracted and stored as a separate scalar value. When a virtual source moves, the system interpolates the minimum-phase spectra (avoiding comb filtering) and independently interpolates the ITD delay line, guaranteeing a continuous, artifact-free transition12.  
To render a binaural signal, the mono input ![][image6] is convolved with the left and right HRIRs. The mathematical definition of discrete linear convolution is:  
![][image7]  
![][image8]  
Time-domain FIR convolution requires ![][image9] operations, which becomes CPU-bound for long filters. Fast convolution via the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) reduces this to ![][image10]. By the convolution theorem, time-domain convolution is equivalent to frequency-domain multiplication. To process continuous audio streams in real-time with low latency, partitioned convolution (overlap-save or overlap-add) is strictly required.  
Anthropometric HRTF prediction attempts to synthesize personalized filters without physical measurement. Machine learning models map physical features (ear shape, head width, extracted via smartphone photographs) to a low-dimensional HRTF latent space13. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) or spherical harmonic decomposition is often used for dimensionality reduction of the HRTF dataset before training the neural network.

## **PART IV: Binaural DSP**

Processing spatial audio requires sophisticated digital signal processing (DSP). Spatial position cannot be simulated merely by simple delay and gain; simple delay lacks the frequency-dependent diffraction effects of the human head, resulting in an unnatural "comb-filtered" phantom image rather than true externalization.  
When applying HRTFs in the frequency domain, the fundamental operation is ![][image11]. The overlap-save algorithm processes the input in blocks. For a filter of length ![][image12] and a block size of ![][image13], the algorithm requires an FFT size of ![][image14].

> 1. The input is buffered into blocks of length ![][image15], overlapping the previous block by ![][image16] samples.  
> 2. The block undergoes a Real-to-Complex FFT.  
> 3. The spectrum is multiplied by the pre-computed frequency-domain HRTF.  
> 4. An Inverse FFT is performed.  
> 5. The first ![][image16] samples (containing circular convolution aliasing) are discarded, and the remaining ![][image13] valid samples are appended to the output stream.

For low-latency applications (like Web Audio), partitioned convolution divides the HRTF into smaller sub-filters. The first few partitions are processed in the time domain or with small FFTs to ensure near-zero latency, while the later tail partitions are processed with large FFTs in background threads to maximize CPU efficiency.

## **PART V: Ambisonics**

Ambisonics provides a scene-based, isotropic representation of a soundfield. Instead of representing discrete speaker channels, it decomposes the soundfield into spherical harmonics.  
B-format (First-Order Ambisonics, or FOA) consists of four channels: ![][image17] (omnidirectional sound pressure), and ![][image18] (directional pressure gradients corresponding to Cartesian axes). A mono signal ![][image19] arriving from azimuth ![][image1] and elevation ![][image20] is encoded into FOA using the following equations (assuming SN3D normalization):  
![][image21]  
![][image22]  
![][image23]  
Normalization conventions dictate the specific gain coefficients. N3D (fully normalized) ensures equal energy across all orders, while SN3D (Schmidt semi-normalized) ensures that no higher-order channel exceeds the peak amplitude of the zeroth-order ![][image17] channel3. The AmbiX format strictly mandates SN3D normalization and ACN (Ambisonic Channel Number) ordering to prevent the clipping issues prevalent in the older FuMa standard.  
Higher Order Ambisonics (HOA) expands this mathematical series. While FOA (order ![][image24]) uses 4 channels, HOA of order ![][image12] requires ![][image25] channels. Increasing the order tightens the spatial rendering precision and pushes the spatial aliasing frequency higher, widening the effective "sweet spot" for loudspeaker reproduction5.  
Binaural rendering of an Ambisonic soundfield is achieved by decoding the spherical harmonics to a virtual loudspeaker array (e.g., a Lebedev grid) and convolving those virtual feeds with the corresponding HRTFs. Alternatively, direct Ambisonic-to-binaural decoding matrices can be computed analytically by expanding the HRTF dataset into spherical harmonics and taking the inner product with the Ambisonic signal channels.

## **PART VI: Object-Based Audio**

Object-based audio abstracts the mix from the reproduction layout. The architecture comprises "beds" (traditional channel-based stems, like a 7.1.2 ambient bed) and "objects" (mono or stereo assets with dynamic metadata).  
The renderer ingests the audio and metadata simultaneously. The metadata defines the object's ![][image26] coordinates, size (spatial spread), and divergence (how energy leaks into adjacent speakers). The renderer computes panning gains in real-time based on the user's specific endpoint. For a 7.1.4 home theater, it executes Vector Base Amplitude Panning (VBAP); for headphones, it executes HRTF convolution.  
This architecture ensures optimal playback on any device, from a massive Dolby Cinema array down to standard stereo headphones, because the spatial intent is preserved in the metadata rather than baked into discrete audio channels1.

## **PART VII: Room Acoustics**

An HRTF applied in an anechoic vacuum sounds unnatural and highly localized inside or near the head. Convincing 3D sound requires the simulation of room acoustics, modeled by the Room Impulse Response (RIR), ![][image27]. RIR convolution, ![][image28], places the source within a virtual environment.  
The RIR contains three distinct temporal phases. The Direct Sound is the initial wavefront. The Early Reflections (typically 0–80 ms) define the physical geometry and boundaries of the room. These are computationally modeled using the Image Source Method (ISM). Introduced by Allen and Berkley (1979), ISM mathematically mirrors the source position across the room's planar boundaries, treating reflections as secondary phantom sources16. Each reflection is delayed based on distance, attenuated by boundary absorption coefficients, and convolved with the specific HRTF corresponding to its angle of arrival.  
The Late Reverberation forms the dense, stochastic tail characterized by the ![][image29] (the time required for energy to decay by 60 dB). Simulating late reverb via ISM requires exponentially increasing computational power. Therefore, algorithmic approaches like Feedback Delay Networks (FDN) are utilized18. An FDN routes the signal through multiple parallel delay lines connected via an orthogonal feedback matrix (such as a Householder matrix).  
Modern spatial audio utilizes the Directional Feedback Delay Network (DFDN). A DFDN groups delay lines by spatial direction and applies a spherical harmonic transform in the feedback loop. This generates anisotropic late reverberation, allowing the ![][image29] to decay at different rates depending on the azimuth and elevation, accurately mimicking real-world spaces with non-uniform acoustic absorption20.

| Acoustic Phase | Physical Phenomenon | Simulation Method | Spatial Consequence |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Direct Sound** | Line-of-sight propagation | Pure delay \+ attenuation | Primary localization (ITD/ILD) |
| **Early Reflections** | First-order boundary bounces | Image Source Method (ISM) | Externalization, source width |
| **Late Reverb** | Diffuse, dense scattering | FDN / DFDN algorithms | Envelopment, room volume perception |

## **PART VIII: Voice and Source Processing**

When processing ordinary 2D audio into spatial 3D audio, the fundamental issue is the lack of isolated stems and metadata. Converting a mono podcast or a stereo song into a spatial scene requires specialized voice and source processing.  
The optimal Voice-to-Spatial pipeline is sequentially structured:

> 1. **Voice Activity Detection (VAD) & Diarization:** Identifies when speech occurs and clusters segments by speaker identity.  
> 2. **Noise Reduction & Dereverberation:** Removes baked-in mono reverberation. Spatializing an already reverberant mono signal causes conflicting spatial cues, destroying externalization. Neural algorithms (e.g., RNNoise) or Wiener filtering are applied to isolate the dry signal.  
> 3. **Source Separation:** Deep neural networks, specifically hybrid Demucs models or SepFormer architectures, decompose complex mixtures into isolated stems (e.g., Vocals, Drums, Bass)22.  
> 4. **Semantic Spatial Placement:** The isolated stems are assigned semantic positions. Vocals are locked to the center-front (0° azimuth, 0° elevation) with a high DRR, while ambient noise and backing instrumentation are decorrelated and pushed to the peripheral hemisphere.

Neural source separation operates by transforming the waveform into a magnitude spectrogram via STFT, processing it through a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) U-Net architecture to predict continuous ratio masks for each stem, and reconstructing the time-domain signal via the Inverse STFT22.

## **PART IX: AI Approaches to Spatial Audio**

Machine learning has revolutionized acoustic scene analysis. To infer spatial positions from raw stereo recordings, models utilize Direction-of-Arrival (DoA) estimation.  
The Spatial Cue-Augmented Log-Spectrogram (SALSA) feature set maps signal power explicitly to source directional cues. SALSA-Lite extracts normalized inter-channel phase differences (IPD) directly from multichannel complex spectrograms25. This circumvents the computationally expensive spatial covariance matrix eigenvector calculations required by the original SALSA method, offering a 30-fold speedup suitable for real-time Sound Event Localization and Detection (SELD)27.  
Furthermore, Generative AI and diffusion models are emerging to synthesize entirely novel Room Impulse Responses from architectural floor plans or image data, allowing dynamic acoustic rendering without physical measurement. However, these models currently suffer from high inference latency, restricting their use to offline preprocessing.

## **PART X: Analysis of Commercial Systems**

Analyzing commercial systems reveals that perceptual plausibility often overrides strict physical accuracy in order to conserve computational resources.

| System | Primary Architecture | Spatial Rendering Approach | Key Distinguishing Feature |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Dolby Atmos for Headphones** | Object \+ Channel Beds | 85% Panning / 15% HRTF Blend | Minimizes HRTF timbral coloration7 |
| **Sony 360 Reality Audio** | Scene \+ Object (MPEG-H) | Full HRTF with Personalization | AI-driven ear scanning for HRTF matching13 |
| **Waves Nx** | Channel Downmix | Virtual Loudspeakers via HRTF | Emphasizes cross-talk cancellation and head tracking29 |
| **Apple Spatial Audio** | Object \+ Channel | Dynamic Head-Tracking HRTF | Tight integration with device IMUs for stable soundfields |

**Dolby Atmos:** Public patents and reverse-engineering research suggest that Dolby Atmos does not apply heavy HRTF convolution to every object. Applying full HRTFs to dozens of objects causes the pinna notches (at 6.5 kHz and 9–10 kHz) to compound, resulting in a hollow, metallic spectral coloration. By heavily blending standard amplitude panning with a slight (15%) HRTF imprint, the system maintains spectral integrity while providing just enough spatial cues to trigger externalization7.  
**Sony 360 Reality Audio / MPEG-H 3D Audio:** Standardized under ISO/IEC 23008-3, this ecosystem is purely object- and scene-based. MPEG-H relies heavily on Metadata Audio Elements (MAE) and the MHAS transport stream, allowing real-time switching and dynamic gain adjustments2. Sony mitigates front/back confusion by allowing users to photograph their ears; an AI algorithm matches the anthropometric data to a database to select a personalized HRTF13.

## **PART XI: Web Application Implementation**

Deploying a professional-grade 3D audio engine via a web browser requires bypassing standard DOM limitations. Traditional JavaScript ScriptProcessorNode is deprecated due to severe latency and main-thread blocking30.  
The architecture must utilize the Web Audio API's AudioWorklet. The audio rendering executes on a dedicated, high-priority audio thread. However, executing complex neural network inference (like Demucs source separation) inside the time budget of an AudioWorklet quantum (typically 128 samples, or \~2.9 ms at 44.1 kHz) will trigger audio dropouts.  
A hybrid browser architecture is strictly required:

> 1. **AI Analysis Thread:** Web Workers run ONNX Runtime Web using the WebGPU backend to execute the Demucs source separation model asynchronously22.  
> 2. **State Management:** Spatial parameters (coordinates from the UI) and processed audio stems are written to a SharedArrayBuffer31. This allows the UI and the audio thread to exchange data with zero serialization overhead, achieving lock-free synchronization via JavaScript Atomics.  
> 3. **DSP Rendering Engine:** The core spatialization logic (convolution, FDN, fractional delays) is written in C++ or Rust and compiled to WebAssembly (WASM) with SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) enabled22. The WASM binary is instantiated directly inside the AudioWorkletProcessor.

This architecture ensures that non-deterministic AI processing remains entirely decoupled from the latency-critical rendering loop, maintaining sub-10ms audio latency31.

## **PART XII: Proposed System Architecture**

Based on the synthesis of academic and commercial research, the following modular architecture is proposed for the independent 2D-to-3D application.  
**MODULE 1: Audio Ingestion & Decoding** Utilizes the WebCodecs API to decode arbitrary formats (MP3, AAC, FLAC) into raw PCM data, resampling to a standardized 48 kHz operating rate to ensure HRTF alignment.  
**MODULE 2: Pre-Processing & Source Separation** Applies a WebGPU-accelerated Demucs model (quantized to INT8 to reduce browser load times from 170MB to \~40MB) to split the input into discrete stems23.  
**MODULE 3: Spatial Scene Generation** Assigns Cartesian coordinates to the separated stems. Implements an 85/15 spatial blend engine (inspired by Dolby Atmos methodologies) where the signal is split into a direct amplitude-panned path and a minimum-phase HRTF convolution path to prevent spectral degradation7.  
**MODULE 4: Distance & Room Engine** Calculates inverse-square attenuation and applies Biquad low-pass filtering for air absorption. Early reflections are mapped via the Image Source Method (ISM), while late reverberation is generated using a 16-channel Directional Feedback Delay Network (DFDN) to synthesize anisotropic room decay20.  
**MODULE 5: Dynamic Movement & Mixing** Handles trajectory interpolation using quaternion math. Implements first-order Thiran fractional delay filters to prevent zipper noise during movement33. Finally, applies EBU R128 loudness normalization and soft clipping before outputting to the Web Audio destination.

## **PART XV: Evaluation and Quality Metrics**

A robust quality-evaluation framework for 2D ![][image55] 3D spatialization must balance objective metrics with subjective psychoacoustic assessment.

* **Objective Metrics:** The Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) and Short-Time Objective Intelligibility (STOI) quantify core signal degradation post-processing. Spectral Distortion (SD) measures the deleterious coloration added by HRTF convolution. Interaural Cross-Correlation (IACC) evaluates the synthesized source width and spatial envelopment.  
* **Subjective Metrics:** The Multiple Stimuli with Hidden Reference and Anchor (MUSHRA) paradigm (ITU-R BS.1534) is strictly required for evaluating spatial localization accuracy, externalization, and overall timbral fidelity39. Evaluators perform blind A/B/X tests comparing the synthesized scene against physical loudspeaker references.

## **PART XVII: Limitations and What Cannot Be Done**

It is essential to acknowledge fundamental physical limitations. When operating on a single mono microphone recording, all spatial information of the original recording space is irreversibly lost.  
A DSP system *cannot* mathematically reconstruct the original acoustic environment of a mono recording; it can only *simulate* a new virtual environment and artificially *synthesize* plausible spatial cues.  
If a stereo track contains heavy mastering compression and limiting, source separation algorithms (like Demucs) will exhibit severe artifacts (phase smearing and musical noise), as the dynamic compression permanently binds the stems together. Attempting to spatialize severely compressed, unseparated audio results in a chaotic, unlocalizable soundfield.  
Furthermore, perfectly universal HRTFs do not exist. Without individualized measurements or anatomical scanning, generic HRTFs will inevitably cause elevated localization errors (particularly elevation and front/back confusion) and inside-the-head localization for the subset of the population whose anthropometry significantly deviates from the dataset mean.

## **PART XVIII: Patents and Intellectual Property**

While this report does not constitute legal advice, architectural design must navigate a dense patent landscape in the spatial audio domain.  
Binaural downmixing of object metadata and specific headphone virtualization pipelines are heavily patented by Dolby Laboratories and DTS40. MPEG-H 3D audio is subject to licensing pools managed by Fraunhofer, Dolby, and Sony40. Furthermore, specific techniques for mitigating comb-filtering during HRTF interpolation—such as phase linearization prior to convolution—are claimed in modern patents (e.g., Gaudio Lab’s US 10,609,504 B2)41.  
By building a pipeline grounded in fundamental acoustics—utilizing the classic Image Source Method, public-domain Feedback Delay Networks, open-source ONNX Demucs models, and standard spherical harmonic Ambisonic math—an engineer can construct a robust, commercial-grade 3D audio engine that rests securely on foundational, unprotected mathematical principles rather than proprietary commercial implementations.

## **PART XIX & XX: Appendices**

### **Iso-Loudness Contours (ISO 226:2023)**

Spatial processing inherently alters the frequency spectrum, which affects perceived loudness. The ISO 226:2023 standard defines the equal-loudness contours (phon curves), updating older Fletcher-Munson data42. The sensitivity of human hearing peaks sharply between 2 kHz and 4 kHz. When applying HRTF equalization, especially to lateral sources that boost the 3 kHz range due to pinna gain, the overall LUFS (Loudness Units relative to Full Scale) will artificially spike. The DSP pipeline must apply an inverse loudness weighting filter prior to the final output stage to prevent jarring volume jumps as objects pan around the listener's head.

### **The SOFA Format Specification**

The Spatially Oriented Format for Acoustics (SOFA), standardized as AES69, is the critical file format for storing HRTFs and BRIRs. It utilizes the NetCDF container structure, representing data natively in multidimensional arrays44. The format specifies SourcePosition (azimuth, elevation, radius) and Data.IR (the impulse responses). A Web Audio implementation requires a dedicated JavaScript or WASM NetCDF parser to extract the Data.IR block, normalize it, extract the minimum-phase and ITD components, and load it into the engine's internal Float32Array buffers for real-time convolution.
